summary: This Royal College of Psychiatrists College Report (CR186, March 2014) sets out a Code of Ethics for good psychiatric practice. It explains that the code defines professional virtues and is grounded in older medical ethics codes and psychiatric guidance, and it adopts a framework of 12 principles, with a summary list of those principles. The report stresses that the good of patients and carers should guide judgement, and that the principles use 'shall' to signal they must be adhered to without exception, though the code does not have the force of law.
one_line: Royal College of Psychiatrists' 2014 Code of Ethics setting out 12 principles for good psychiatric practice.
key_facts: College Report CR186, titled Good Psychiatric Practice: Code of Ethics, was published by the Royal College of Psychiatrists in March 2014.
The report was approved by the College Policy Committee in September 2013 and was due for review in 2016.
The Declaration of Geneva (Physician's Oath), first stated in 1948, updated the Hippocratic Oath.
The Nuremberg Code of 1947 governs human experimentation and has been modified by various revisions of the Declaration of Helsinki.
The General Medical Council (GMC) sets the ethical standards which guide general medical practice in the UK.
The Code's 11 principles were used as a framework with permission from the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists (2010).
The introduction states that the central ethical focus of judgement must be the good of patients and carers.
The 12 principles are open to future revision and are not intended to replace other ethical or legal guidance to doctors.
The code does not have the force of law and cannot be used to justify breaching legal contracts or duties.
The code uses the term 'shall' rather than 'should' to indicate that its principles must be adhered to without variation or exception.
Principle 1: Psychiatrists shall respect the essential humanity and dignity of every patient.
Principle 4: Psychiatrists shall maintain the confidentiality of patients and their families.
Principle 5: Psychiatrists shall seek valid consent from their patients before undertaking any procedure or treatment.
Principle 8: Psychiatrists shall comply with ethical principles embodied in national and international guidelines governing research.
Principle 12: Psychiatrists shall work to improve mental health services and promote community awareness of mental illness, reducing the effects of stigma and discrimination.
